title: Drowning: rescue and first care
asks: someone is drowning how do I rescue them
pulled from the water and not breathing
kid went under in the lake and is unresponsive
do I pump the water out of the lungs
how to save a drowning person without drowning myself
pt submerged pulled out not breathing
he swallowed water and is coughing is he ok
answer: Call for help, and keep yourself safe: rescuer safety is a priority. An untrained rescuer or weaker swimmer should use flotation devices, ropes or paddles instead of swimming to the person.

Rescue options: reach with an object from the shore or boat; throw a rope or something that floats; row or paddle a small craft to them; tow them to shore. Go into the water only as a last resort, and only if it is within your skill.
Out of the water, place the person so that the head and feet are at the same level.

If the person is unconscious and not breathing: begin with 5 rescue breaths, then act on the pulse. No pulse: continue with cycles of 30 chest compressions and 2 rescue breaths. A pulse: give rescue breaths only, with no chest compressions. The JTS drowning guideline says drowning patients whose circulation has not stopped will often respond to rescue breaths alone, and that absence of a pulse necessitates starting basic life support (CPR). If the person has been in cold water, check for breathing and a pulse for a full minute (HHS ship's medical manual). How to check for a pulse, and the steps for rescue breaths and CPR, are on this library's card 'CPR for an adult'.
Sweep sand, seaweed or other material out of the mouth with a finger only if you can see it.

An unconscious person who cannot keep their own airway open should be placed in the recovery position (on their side) to reduce the risk of breathing in vomit. Vomiting is common with rescue breaths and CPR after drowning: use the recovery position whenever you are able.
Keep the person warm: dry and insulate them to prevent heat loss.

Everyone who needed resuscitation, even rescue breaths alone, should go to a hospital for evaluation and monitoring, even if alert and stable. Also evacuate anyone who was unresponsive in the water or has trouble breathing or other breathing symptoms.
warnings: Do not use abdominal thrusts (the Heimlich maneuver) or a head-down position to get water out: they decrease ventilation and increase the risk of vomiting. The Heimlich maneuver has no role unless a solid object (not water or vomit) blocks the airway and breaths cannot otherwise get in.
After drowning in cold water, rewarm the person while CPR continues: no victim should be declared dead until they are rewarmed and fail to respond to CPR.
In the water, chest compressions are not effective and should not be attempted. Give rescue breaths in the water only when the person cannot be got out quickly.
Do not delay rescue breaths to immobilize the neck unless the circumstances suggest a spinal injury (diving, boat accident, fall from height).
Start resuscitation unless there are clear signs of death: people have survived prolonged submersion, especially in cold conditions.
After immersion in water, breathing problems can develop several hours later: watch the person closely.

quotes.text: Rescuer safety is a priority. Untrained rescuers or weaker swimmers should utilize alternative means of rescue such as the use of flotation devices, ropes, or paddles.

1. Reach with an object from the safety of the shore or ship. 2. Throw an object like a rope or flotation devices (this may help the victim stay afloat or the search and rescue team locate the victim.) 3. Row (or paddle) a smaller craft to the victim if they are too far from shore to reach or have a floatation device thrown. The rescuer should ideally stay out of the water. 4. Tow them into shore or away from danger in the water (i.e. swift water rescue). 5. Go into the water (as a last resort) to rescue the victim if this is within the rescuer's skill set.
In water rescue, breaths should only be done when rapid extraction is NOT feasible. In water, chest compressions are NOT effective and should not be attempted.

Call for help and encourage patient to move away from danger.16-17 ▪ Place the patient so that the head and feet are at the same level. If rescuing a patient from the shoreline, place them parallel to the shoreline. ▪ Airway, Breathing, Circulation. If unconscious and not breathing, begin with 5 rescue breaths, then continue with traditional basic life support utilizing a ratio of 30 compressions and 2 rescue breaths. Five breaths are used initially as a recruitment maneuver. Drowning patients without circulatory arrest will often respond to rescue breaths alone.
While pulses may be difficult to identify due to hypothermia or hypotension, absence of a pulse necessitates initiation of Basic Life Support/Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS) protocols.
j. if no pulse or breathing, continue CPR; k. if pulse but no breathing, continue rescue breathing; and l. if pulse and breathing present, place victim in recovery position (on side).

The treatment of all near-drowning cases involves the careful removal of the victim from the water (taking care to protect the neck in the event of spinal injury), assessment for breathing and pulse (check for a full minute, if the victim has been in cold water), clearing the airway of any water, vomit or other objects), CPR, administration of oxygen, and defibrillation if necessary when appropriately trained medical personnel and equipment are available.

Rescue breaths and CPR represent significant risk of emesis in drowning victims (65% of those requiring rescue and 88% of those receiving chest compressions).10 Placing patients in the recovery position as able can reduce the risk of subsequent aspiration.

All victims of drowning who require resuscitation (including rescue breathing alone) should be transported to the hospital for evaluation and monitoring, even those who are alert and demonstrate hemodynamic and respiratory stability at the scene of initial injury.

Aggressive resuscitation attempts should be initiated unless clear signs of death or as limited by operational requirements. Patients have survived prolonged submersion historically, especially in the hypothermic environment.

Assess patency of the patient's airway; consider foreign bodies unique to drowning injuries such as sand or seaweed and perform finger sweep if there is a visible obstruction. ▪ If the patient is unconscious and unable to maintain their own airway, place the patient in the recovery position (lateral recumbent) to minimize risk of aspiration.
Avoid head down positioning or abdominal thrusts as they decrease ventilation and increase risk of vomiting, which can lead to aspiration. Heimlich maneuver is NO LONGER recommended for drowning.

Keep the victim warm (use core temperature instead of infrared devices - a low range refrigerator thermometer may be necessary). Stabilize body temperature - dry and insulate the patient to prevent heat loss.

Evacuation: Evacuate if victim required resuscitation, was unresponsive in the water, or has dyspnea or other respiratory symptoms. ▪ Continue resuscitation and transport to higher level of care unless there are obvious signs of death.

Unnecessary cervical spine immobilization can impede delivery of rescue breaths via time of application and reduced airway opening. Routine stabilization of the cervical spine in the absence of circumstances that suggest a spinal injury (diving, boat accident, and fall from height) is not recommended.
Following immersion in water (drowning), a person may develop late signs of breathing problems after several hours and should be observed closely.

In clearing the airway prior to CPR, do not perform the Heimlich maneuver! The Heimlich maneuver has no role in drowning resuscitation, unless a solid foreign body obstructs the airway (this does not mean water or vomit) and ventilation is otherwise impossible.
Hypothermic near-drowning victims should be rewarmed while CPR is ongoing, and no victim should be declared dead until they are rewarmed and fail to respond to CPR or other resuscitative efforts.

conflict: WHEN TO STOP (the card gives no stop time): JTS Drowning Management 2025 says in-water rescue becomes body recovery after more than 60 minutes of submersion, resuscitation of a non-hypothermic patient may stop after 30 minutes of CPR without return of circulation, and a hypothermic patient is rewarmed to 30-34 °C before stopping if still without a heartbeat for more than 20 minutes; HHS Ship's Medicine Chest 2003 says no victim should be declared dead until rewarmed and unresponsive to CPR. NECK: JTS says routine neck immobilization is not recommended unless the circumstances suggest spinal injury (diving, boat accident, fall from height); Ship's Medicine Chest says remove the victim carefully, protecting the neck in the event of spinal injury (compatible). PULSE CHECK (now on the card, in step 4): Ship's Medicine Chest says check breathing and pulse for a full minute if the victim has been in cold water; JTS gives no time, but says pulses 'may be difficult to identify due to hypothermia or hypotension'. FEMA P-2064 (2020) has no drowning first aid. COMPRESSIONS ONLY WHEN THERE IS NO PULSE (step 4, changed 2026-11-25 to match the card cpr-adult; the reviewer recommended it on this card and required it on that one): JTS Drowning 2025, Initial Resuscitation, says 'If unconscious and not breathing, begin with 5 rescue breaths, then continue with traditional basic life support utilizing a ratio of 30 compressions and 2 rescue breaths' and, two sentences on, 'Drowning patients without circulatory arrest will often respond to rescue breaths alone'; under Circulation it says 'absence of a pulse necessitates initiation of Basic Life Support/Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS) protocols'. The earlier step told the reader to give compressions after the 5 breaths whatever the pulse. The rule 'a pulse but not breathing: rescue breaths only' is stated outright by the HHS 2003 crew standard ('if pulse but no breathing, continue rescue breathing') and is the rule on the card cpr-adult. A possible other reading, for the reviewer and owner: JTS Table 2 (CPR in the drowning patient) lists under 'When to initiate' a 'Patient with respiratory distress or respiratory arrest' and 'Submerged for < 60 min with no obvious physical evidence of death', and does not mention the pulse; the card takes 'CPR' there in the wide sense of resuscitation (rescue breaths for someone not breathing, compressions when the Circulation paragraph's condition, no pulse, is met). From outside the kit (the reviewer's notes on cpr-adult): current lay-rescuer guidance skips the pulse check, and a mistaken pulse is the main way a pulse-based rule can harm. Dependency for the owner: step 4 points to the card cpr-adult ('CPR for an adult') for how to check a pulse and for the rescue-breath and CPR steps; approve this card together with that one, or remove the pointer sentence.

review.notes: Re-review 2026-11-25 (claude-opus-5-5 xhigh). Fail (one problem). Previous recommendations taken up: step 4 now gives compressions only with no pulse and rescue breaths only with a pulse, attributed to JTS Drowning 2025 (Initial Resuscitation and Circulation paragraphs, checked in context), plus HHS's full-minute check after cold water, attributed; this agrees with cpr-adult A4 and A14, and the pointer uses the exact title 'CPR for an adult'. JTS Table 2: the card's reading is right and the table need not be shown: the Circulation paragraph sends the reader to Table 2 from its 'absence of a pulse' sentence; Table 3 grades 'Apnea +Pulse' (grade 5) apart from 'Apnea without Pulse' (grade 6); and read literally Table 2 would start CPR on a breathing patient in respiratory distress, which no kit source supports. Problem (pulse rule; incomplete against cpr-adult): 'then act on the pulse ... A pulse: give rescue breaths only, with no chest compressions' is one check with no re-check. cpr-adult's same branch ends 'keep re-checking the pulse, and start CPR if it is lost', a clause the first cpr-adult review required. A drowned person who is not breathing but has a pulse can lose it during rescue breathing (JTS Table 3 gives that grade a mortality of 31-44%), and the dependency note offers the owner removing the pointer, after which this card must stand alone. Fix: 'A pulse: give rescue breaths only, with no chest compressions; keep re-checking the pulse, and start compressions if it is lost', extending the HHS quote to begin at 'i. after performing 1 minute CPR, reassess breathing and pulse' as on cpr-adult; the JTS 'absence of a pulse necessitates initiation of Basic Life Support' quote already supports starting compressions. Everything else unchanged and still faithful (rescuer safety, reach-throw-row-tow-go, level positioning, finger sweep, recovery position and vomiting, warmth, hospital and evacuation, the six warnings); kind protocol; asks answered; no PDF junk. Optional: (a) after cold water, say in what order the full-minute check and the 5 breaths go, so the minute is not read as a wait before any breath (JTS Breathing: 'Immediately perform five rescue breaths in a patient who remains unconscious and in respiratory arrest'; HHS: check breathing and pulse for a full minute; the kit gives no order); (b) add Table 3 to the conflict's Table 2 note as the stronger support for the card's reading. previous review: (verdict pass, by claude-opus-5-5 (xhigh), independent review 2026-11-24) Confirmed in context: JTS Drowning Management 2025 (rescuer safety; reach-throw-row-tow-go; no compressions in water, breaths only if extraction is slow; head and feet level; 5 rescue breaths then 30:2; vomiting and recovery position; finger sweep only if visible; no head-down or abdominal thrusts; keep warm; hospital for anyone resuscitated; evacuation criteria; no routine neck immobilization; resuscitate unless obvious death), WHO (late breathing problems), HHS (no Heimlich unless solid object; rewarm during CPR, not dead until warm). Call for help is first. Stop-time, neck and pulse-check differences are listed. No PDF junk. Recommended: JTS also says 'Drowning patients without circulatory arrest will often respond to rescue breaths alone'; add 'if there is a pulse, keep giving rescue breaths only' so compressions are not started on a beating heart (same gap as cpr-adult); HHS's full-minute pulse check in cold water is worth showing on the card.
